Chapter Two: The Carceral State—Prisons, Policing, and the Logic of Control
You know, there’s a certain chill that settles in when we start talking about prisons. For some folks, it’s a distant thing—something that happens to other people, in some other neighborhood. But for others, it’s right there, every single day. Maybe it’s a loved one behind bars, a police car always parked on the corner, or just that feeling of being watched.
The carceral state—it isn’t just about concrete buildings and locked doors. It’s really about how our society decides who’s dangerous, who gets pushed aside, and who’s allowed to be free.
Think about this: in so many cities these days, the line between police and military has almost disappeared. You see armored vehicles rolling down quiet streets, officers dressed in camouflage, and cameras keeping an eye on everything. The reason we’re given is always the same—safety, order, protection. But for people living under that constant gaze, it feels like something very different—a message that their lives are considered a threat, that just existing means being controlled.
The rise of mass incarceration in the United States? It didn’t just fall out of the sky. It was built, step by step, through laws and policies that went after the most vulnerable. We’re talking about the war on drugs, mandatory minimum sentences, and giving police more and more power. All of this added up to a system that locks up millions—disproportionately Black and brown people. Prisons became the answer to problems that could’ve been met with care, investment, and understanding. But instead, entire communities got labeled as dangerous, left carrying the heavy weight of suspicion.
And this way of thinking—it’s not just an American story. You’ll find it in other places, too. Look at Palestine, for example. There, detention, checkpoints, and constant surveillance are used to control people seen as threatening. The language might change, but the result is the same: people get reduced to numbers, and their basic humanity is denied.
For folks caught up in all this, the impact goes deep. Imagine a teenager, stopped and searched on their way to school—they learn to move carefully, to shrink themselves, to avoid standing out. Or a mother, waiting for hours to see her son in prison—her hope rubbing up against exhaustion. That feeling of being watched, judged, and punished shapes how people see themselves and where they fit in the world.
Most of us don’t even notice how deeply this carceral logic has seeped into our everyday lives. Schools set up zero-tolerance policies, suspending kids for things that barely matter. Homelessness and mental illness get treated as crimes, not as issues that deserve compassion. It’s like the boundaries of the prison just keep expanding—moving into our homes, our schools, our streets.
But here’s the thing—even with all this machinery, resistance is always there. Families come together to support loved ones behind bars. Activists push back, demanding an end to solitary confinement, to cash bail, to the endless cycle of punishment. The call for abolition—getting rid of prisons, of police, of the systems that make them seem necessary—it’s getting louder. And it isn’t just about tearing down walls. It’s about dreaming up a world where safety is built on care, not control.
The fight against the carceral state isn’t simple. It means facing up to the fears and assumptions that make punishment feel like the only option. It means asking some tough questions about what justice really is, and who actually gets to decide. But the more people begin to see how all these things are connected—from Ferguson to Palestine, from prisons to poverty—the more real the possibility of change becomes.
